newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to devise rules on trade with HK, Macau.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to devise rules on trade with HK, Macau.

text.p: Taiwan is expected to devise rules governing its multi-billion dollar trade and investment activities in Hong Kong and Macau after their respective handovers to rival China, officials said on Wednesday.

"After passage of the Hong Kong-Macau Relations Act, a set of rules are needed to govern our trade and investment activities after the handovers of the two places," said Tsai Lien-sheng, executive secretary of the Economics Ministry's Investment Commission.

Hong Kong will revert to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, 1997, after 150 years of British colonial rule. The enclave of Macau will be handed back to the mainland on December 20, 1999, closing the book on Portuguese control dating back to 1557.
Taiwan's parliament on March 18 approved the Hong Kong-Macau Relations Act, laying the legal framework for continued relations with post-handover Hong Kong.
But the act does not stipulate specific guidelines for trade and investment, government officials said.

"A cross-department meeting in which leaders from relevant government organisations will be held tomorrow (Thursday) to discuss the mapping out of trade and investment rules," Tsai told Reuters by telephone.
He said the rules would also include fines and punishments for businesses which violate the act.

Under the government's plan, Taiwan would maintain trade and investment activities with Hong Kong under current conditions, avoiding its long-standing ban on direct contact with rival China, officials said.

But the guidelines would include certain stipulations to ensure that investments in Hong Kong, the main conduit for huge amounts of Taiwanese investment in China, would not endanger Taiwan's national security, officials said.

"Basically, we will treat the two areas (Hong Kong and Macau) as special administrative zones different from that of mainland China," William Li, director of Hong Kong and Macau affairs under the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, told Reuters.
Trade and investment activities with the two territories would remain as open as possible, Li said.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war ended in 1949, and Taipei's Nationalist government has prohibited its businesses to directly invest in or trade with the mainland.

But more than 30,000 Taiwan firms are estimated to have channeled as much as US$30 billion to the mainland indirectly through third places like Hong Kong since the Nationalists eased the ban during the late 1980s.
Taiwan's exports to Hong Kong in 1996 stood at US$26.8 billion -- most destined for China -- while imports totalled just US$1.7 billion.
